clue.text: Example of fashionable posture

parts.note: something fashionable is said to be in
a posture is a stance, the way one stands

explanation.surface: A model striking a voguish pose as an illustration of style.
explanation.definitionFit: An instance is a single case cited to illustrate something, which is what an example is.

clue.text: I've nothing to eat but antiseptic

parts.note: I have nothing: the letter I with O, a zero, beside it
to dine is to eat

explanation.surface: A hungry person with an empty larder has only disinfectant in the cupboard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'but' only joins the pieces to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Tincture of this element is a classic germ-killing wound dressing.

clue.text: It's a quick break-through, by the sound of it

definitions.text: It's a quick break-through, by the sound of it

parts.words: It's a quick break-through, by the sound of it
parts.note: a rapid breakthrough of the sound barrier, heard as a loud bang

explanation.surface: A sudden advance that seems, from the noise, to have been a breakthrough.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by the sound of it' reads as 'apparently' but means the barrier of sound that a supersonic aircraft breaks.
explanation.definitionFit: The bang heard when an aircraft passes supersonic speed, crossing the sound barrier.

clue.text: Can a claim be made for obsolete scient: apparatus?

indicators.note: made here means fashioned into something new, so the letters are reformed

explanation.surface: A question whether one may claim credit for an outdated piece of lab kit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'made' signals the anagram of CLAIM BE; 'Can a' and 'for' only join the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: An alembic is an old distilling vessel used by alchemists, long replaced by modern stills.

clue.text: It performs here on Sundays

parts.note: the group of singers who perform at services, and also the part of the church where they sit

explanation.surface: A remark about a show staged every Sunday.
explanation.walkthrough: The word means both the body of singers ('It performs') and the chancel area they sit in ('here').
explanation.definitionFit: A church's band of singers sings at Sunday services, and its seats in the chancel bear the same name.

clue.text: Cuts out smart seats

explanation.surface: A tailor who snips fabric and also upholsters fine chairs.
explanation.walkthrough: In a British theatre the stalls are the ground-floor seats nearest the stage, traditionally the dear ones.
explanation.definitionFit: An engine that cuts out is said to stall; theatre stalls are the expensive ground-floor places.

clue.text: Teams of acrobats in the Army, we hear

indicators.note: we hear means the word is judged by how it is spoken

parts.note: soldiers in the army are troops

explanation.surface: Gymnastic squads serving among the soldiers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'we hear' says that TROOPS, the soldiers, sounds like the word for touring companies of performers.
explanation.definitionFit: A troupe is a touring company of performers, such as circus tumblers.

clue.text: Protective layer inside a big ship

explanation.surface: Lining fitted inside an ocean-going vessel for protection.
explanation.definitionFit: An inner lining protects a coat or a bin; an ocean passenger vessel is also called one.

clue.text: One that makes leisurely progress in a showy jumper

explanation.surface: Someone ambling along wearing a flashy pullover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jumper' is not a pullover but a horse: Stroller was a famous show-jumping pony ridden by Marion Coakes in the 1960s.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who ambles is a stroller; Stroller was a celebrated British show-jumping pony.

clue.text: Transferred according to subscription

explanation.surface: Property handed over in line with the terms of a signed agreement.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as 'as signed', the word means in accordance with a signature, a subscription being a name signed.
explanation.definitionFit: Property assigned has been made over to another; 'as signed' means in line with what was signed.

clue.text: This play should get good notices on the road

definitions.text: This play should get good notices on the road

parts.words: This play should get good notices on the road
parts.note: read as theatre, a touring show hoping for kind reviews; read as traffic, a hazardous bend that ought to carry plenty of warning signs

explanation.surface: A touring production hoping for warm reviews from critics in each town.
explanation.walkthrough: The title is a 1932 J. B. Priestley play; 'notices' are both reviews and roadside warning signs, and 'on the road' is both touring and on the highway.
explanation.definitionFit: Dangerous Corner is a J. B. Priestley stage drama, and a hazardous bend is just the sort of spot that warrants warning signs.

clue.text: Can I rob the islands?

annotationWithheld.why: Can I rob the islands? (7): an anagram of CAN I ROB with no anagram indicator word in the clue (only the question mark), so the op has no indicator the check can accept

clue.text: Risk King Emperor being caught by sliced drive

indicators.note: something caught by another is held within it, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: to drive is to impel; a sliced drive is still a drive, the golf word hinting that it is cut open
R for Rex and I for Imperator, the King Emperor title on old British coins

explanation.surface: A golfer gambles that a royal spectator will be hit by a badly sliced tee shot.
explanation.walkthrough: The golf picture misleads: a sliced shot sounds like a bad drive, but 'drive' is simply propel, and 'being caught by' wraps that verb round the King Emperor's initials from old coinage.
explanation.definitionFit: To imperil something is to put it in danger, which is to risk it.

clue.text: Indian snakeskin shoe ?

parts.note: a soft leather slipper of Native American origin, which also shares its name with a venomous American pit viper, hence the snake

explanation.surface: A North American slipper made from the hide of a serpent.
explanation.walkthrough: The word names both a soft Native American shoe and a pit viper (the water moccasin), so the question mark marks a shoe that is also a snake.
explanation.definitionFit: A moccasin is a soft heelless Native American shoe, and also a venomous North American pit viper.

clue.text: School for seedsmen ?

parts.note: the Latin for seed is semen, so a college for priests is read as a nursery for seeds

explanation.surface: A training college for people who sell garden seeds.
explanation.walkthrough: The word comes from Latin seminarium, a seed plot, from semen 'seed'; it now means a college training priests.
explanation.definitionFit: A seminary is a college for training clergy, its name from the Latin for a seed bed.

clue.text: "The —— has withered from the lake" (Keats)

definitions.text: The —— has withered from the lake" (Keats)

parts.words: The —— has withered from the lake
parts.note: a gap in a line of verse to be filled with the missing word, here a waterside grass-like plant

explanation.surface: A line from a Romantic poem with one word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: The line is from Keats's 'La Belle Dame sans Merci': the missing word is the grass-like plant of marshes and lake edges.
explanation.definitionFit: Sedge is a grassy plant of wet ground, which Keats pictures as dying back by the lakeside in his ballad.

clue.text: Cheat the darlings out of these possessions

parts.note: to do someone is to cheat them
minions are favourites or darlings

explanation.surface: A swindler robs favourite children of their belongings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of' only links the pieces; 'Cheat ... out of' reads as one verb but is split.
explanation.definitionFit: Dominions are territories held by a sovereign state, its overseas holdings.

clue.text: Destructive but favourable criticism

explanation.surface: A review that is both ruinous and full of praise.
explanation.definitionFit: Smashing describes breaking things to pieces, and as British slang it is a word of high praise.

clue.text: Many a doctor has a source of poison

parts.note: M is the Roman numeral for a thousand, so many
MB is Bachelor of Medicine, a doctor's degree

explanation.surface: Lots of physicians possess a supply of something toxic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has' only joins the pieces; the snake is the source of the venom.
explanation.definitionFit: The mamba is a deadly African snake, so a producer of venom.

clue.text: Leading seaman in the rear rank, maybe

definitions.text: Leading seaman in the rear rank, maybe

parts.words: Leading seaman in the rear rank, maybe
parts.note: a naval title of a senior officer, one grade of which is called rear

explanation.surface: A sailor of senior standing who nonetheless stands at the back of the line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leading seaman' is a junior naval rate, but here it means a commanding officer; a rear admiral is one grade of that rank.
explanation.definitionFit: A flag officer commands a fleet, so is a top seafarer; rear is one of his grades.

clue.text: Little bits of mod music, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps says these letters might be arranged otherwise, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Snatches of sixties Mod pop played here and there.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' signals that the letters of MOD MUSIC are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A modicum is a small quantity, so several of them are small amounts.

clue.text: Hire a hydrographer

explanation.surface: An advertisement to engage a marine surveyor.
explanation.walkthrough: A hydrographer charts the sea, so is literally one who charts.
explanation.definitionFit: To charter a boat is to hire it; a sea surveyor makes nautical maps.

clue.text: Fish out of German water

indicators.note: out of here means put out of order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: Wasser is the German for water

explanation.surface: A fish landed from a river in Germany.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of' signals an anagram of WASSER, the German word supplied by 'German water', not printed letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A wrasse is a brightly coloured marine fish of rocky coasts.

clue.text: Child's winter model-abominable!

explanation.surface: A child's frosty figure in the garden that turns out to be horrible.
explanation.walkthrough: The Abominable Snowman is the yeti, so 'abominable' calls up the same word.
explanation.definitionFit: Children build figures from packed flakes in the garden; the yeti is called the Abominable one of these.

clue.text: Cattle-unit on dry hay in Surrey

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece on another sits above it

parts.note: an ox is a single head of cattle
to ted is to spread hay out to dry

explanation.surface: A single beast of the herd on drying hay at a farm in Surrey.
explanation.walkthrough: Oxted is a town in Surrey, a county south of London; 'ted' is a farming word for tossing hay to dry.
explanation.definitionFit: Oxted is a market town in the English county south of London.

clue.text: Author of "The Shape of Things to Come"?

definitions.text: Author of "The Shape of Things to Come"?

parts.words: Author of "The Shape of Things to Come"
parts.note: the book is by H. G. Wells, but read literally the writer of the shape of things to come is whoever lays out future schemes

explanation.surface: A quiz question about who wrote a famous science-fiction book.
explanation.walkthrough: The Shape of Things to Come is H. G. Wells's novel; the question mark sends you from the novelist to anyone who designs the future.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who draws up schemes and layouts for towns or projects decides how the future will look.

clue.text: Turn tap back a point 'or the rice

indicators.note: Turn makes the word tap face the other way, so it is read in reverse
back says the a and point pieces come in reverse order

parts.note: N, north, is a point of the compass

explanation.surface: Instructions to turn a tap and then move back a notch while cooking rice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn' reverses TAP to PAT, and 'back' turns A and N into NA.
explanation.definitionFit: Patna is a long-grain rice named after the city in Bihar, India.

clue.text: From what. Sibyl says, more than one of these is possible

definitions.text: From what. Sibyl says, more than one of these is possible

parts.words: From what. Sibyl says, more than one of these is possible
parts.note: a prophetess speaks in riddles, so her words can be read in several ways

explanation.surface: A remark on how ambiguous an oracle's pronouncements tend to be.
explanation.walkthrough: A sibyl was an ancient prophetess whose sayings were famously open to several readings.
explanation.definitionFit: Readings or explanations of meaning; an oracle's ambiguous words admit many of them.

clue.text: Airborne attacker makes the tribe smart

parts.note: Gad is one of the twelve tribes of Israel
fly is slang for smart or knowing

explanation.surface: A flying raider causes stinging pain to a whole clan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'makes' just joins the pieces; 'smart' looks like the verb to sting but is the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: A horsefly that bites livestock is an insect assailant in the air.

clue.text: Design for the island of Jersey ?

definitions.text: Design for the island of Jersey ?

parts.words: Design for the island of Jersey
parts.note: read as knitwear, a patterned style for a woolly jumper; read literally, a lovely island such as the Channel Island

explanation.surface: Plans drawn up for the Channel Island off Normandy.
explanation.walkthrough: A jersey is a knitted jumper, and the Shetland island's colourful knitting pattern is famous; the words also describe a beautiful island.
explanation.definitionFit: A multicoloured Shetland knitting pattern used on jumpers, and literally a pretty island like Jersey.
